title: sorted()
summary: Return a new sorted list from any iterable, leaving the input untouched.
description: The counterpart to `list.sort()`, which sorts in place and returns None. `key` is a function mapping each element to the value actually compared, and is called **once per element** rather than once per comparison.

parameters.name: iterable
parameters.description: Anything iterable, not just a list.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Extracts the value to order by.

raises.when: Elements are not mutually comparable, e.g. mixing str and int.

examples.title: A tuple key sorts by several fields
Descending one field, ascending another
examples.code:
people = [{'n': 'Ada', 's': 91}, {'n': 'Alan', 's': 78}]
print([p['n'] for p in sorted(people, key=lambda p: (-p['s'], p['n']))])

real_world_usage: Leaderboards, log lines by timestamp, and giving API responses a deterministic order so pagination is stable and tests are not flaky.

common_mistakes.fix: Pass the function itself: key=len. Calling it invokes len with no arguments.

common_mistakes.mistake: Trying to negate a string to reverse it
common_mistakes.fix: Only numbers can be negated. Do two stable sorts instead — least significant field first.
They differ when keys tie: reverse=True preserves the original order of equal elements, reversing afterwards flips it.

performance_notes: Timsort: O(n log n) worst case, approaching O(n) on nearly sorted data, and stable. The key function costs O(n) calls. If you only need the extremes, min, max or heapq.nlargest are O(n).
security_notes: Do not sort by a user-supplied field name passed to getattr — validate against an allowlist. Unbounded sorts of untrusted input are a CPU and memory vector.
